course.title: MITRE ATT&CK
course.description: A practical, research-driven course on the MITRE ATT&CK knowledge base and its operational use. It teaches the current ATT&CK hierarchy, domains, CTI objects, evidence-backed mapping, Navigator, modern Detection Strategies and Analytics, Data Components, threat hunting, STIX 2.1 automation, adversary emulation, purple-team validation, version management, and a defensive capstone. The course emphasizes reproducibility, provenance, safe authorized labs, and meaningful defensive outcomes rather than checklist completion.
prerequisites: Basic cybersecurity concepts and common attack/defense terminology.
Basic Windows/Linux process, authentication, networking, and log knowledge.
Ability to read JSON and use a command line.
Python 3 fundamentals recommended for automation and the capstone.
learningOutcomes: Explain tactics, techniques, sub-techniques, domains, platforms, and major ATT&CK CTI objects.
Map observed behavior to ATT&CK with evidence, confidence, and provenance.
Create and interpret Navigator layers for threat intelligence and defensive coverage.
Use Detection Strategies, Analytics, and Data Components in current ATT&CK defensive workflows.
Design ATT&CK-aligned threat-hunting hypotheses and validation plans.
Query ATT&CK as STIX 2.1 data and resolve relationships programmatically.
Manage ATT&CK versions and translate legacy terminology into current concepts.
Design safe adversary-emulation and purple-team validation exercises.
Build and audit a reproducible ATT&CK automation workflow.

modules.title: ATT&CK Foundations and Scope
modules.description: Build a precise model of ATT&CK, its hierarchy, domains, platforms, and release lifecycle.

lessons.title: What ATT&CK Is
lessons.description: ATT&CK is a knowledge base of adversary behavior based on real-world observations.
learningObjectives: distinguish behavior from a linear attack checklist

notes.text: ATT&CK categorizes adversary behavior. It is not a mandatory checklist and does not claim to capture every possible behavior.

items: Tactics describe why an adversary acts.
Techniques and sub-techniques describe how behavior achieves an objective.
Local evidence remains necessary for incident conclusions.

practicals.title: Classify ATT&CK layers
practicals.description: Separate objective, behavior, and implementation context.
steps: Classify “obtain credentials”, “credential dumping”, and a named tool.
practicals.solution: Objective is tactic-level; credential dumping is behavior; the named tool is software/context. Verify exact IDs in the current catalog.

quiz.question: What does a tactic represent?
quiz.explanation: A tactic is the adversary objective or reason.

summary: ATT&CK is a behavior knowledge base, not a complete attack lifecycle.

lessons.title: Tactics, Techniques, Sub-Techniques
lessons.description: Learn ATT&CK hierarchy and evidence-driven specificity.

notes.text: Tactics are the why; techniques are the how; sub-techniques refine a parent behavior. A technique may support multiple tactical objectives.
Do not choose a sub-technique merely because it is familiar. Specificity must be supported by evidence.

practicals.title: Map an incident fragment
practicals.description: Map a short behavior description to a current technique.
steps: Record ID, rationale, evidence, and confidence.
practicals.solution: Select the narrowest mapping supported by the evidence and explicitly reject unsupported specificity.

quiz.question: Which is most specific?
quiz.explanation: A sub-technique refines a parent technique.

summary: Precision should follow evidence.

lessons.title: Domains, Platforms, and Matrices
lessons.description: Scope analysis correctly across Enterprise, Mobile, and ICS.

notes.text: ATT&CK maintains Enterprise, Mobile, and ICS domains. Enterprise includes traditional enterprise and cloud technologies; Mobile covers Android/iOS; ICS models industrial-control behavior.

practicals.title: Select the domain
practicals.description: Classify Windows enterprise, Android, and industrial-control scenarios.
practicals.solution: Windows enterprise → Enterprise; Android → Mobile; industrial control → ICS.

quiz.question: Which domain covers industrial control systems?
quiz.explanation: ICS is the industrial control systems domain.

summary: Domain selection affects applicability and interpretation.

lessons.title: Versions and Change Management
lessons.description: Make ATT&CK analyses reproducible as the catalog evolves.

notes.text: MITRE lists v19.2 as the current ATT&CK release as of September 2026. The August 2026 Agile release updated Groups and Software for Enterprise.
Historical counts and structures must not be presented as current without checking the release.

practicals.title: Pin an ATT&CK version
steps: Record version, domain, retrieval date, and source.
Explain why an older release may be required for a historical case.
practicals.solution: Example: attack_version=v19.2; domain=Enterprise; retrieved=2026-09-07; source=attack.mitre.org.

quiz.question: Why record ATT&CK version?
quiz.explanation: ATT&CK content and structure are maintained over time.

summary: Version pinning prevents silent semantic drift.

modules.title: ATT&CK Objects and CTI Mapping
modules.description: Read technique pages and relate Groups, Software, Campaigns, Mitigations, and evidence.

lessons.title: Reading a Technique Page
lessons.description: Extract operationally useful information from a technique page.

items: Inspect description, tactics, platforms, procedure examples, mitigations, detection content, and references.
Procedure examples connect documented behavior to named groups/software.

practicals.title: Technique worksheet
steps: Record ID, tactics, platforms, description, procedure examples, references.
State what local evidence would support it.
practicals.solution: Use the live page and preserve its references.

quiz.question: What do procedure examples provide?
quiz.explanation: They connect behavior to documented group/software activity.

summary: Technique pages are research starting points, not substitutes for local evidence.

lessons.title: Groups, Software, and Campaigns
lessons.description: Use CTI objects and relationships without overclaiming attribution.

notes.text: Groups, Software, and Campaigns are CTI objects connected by ATT&CK relationships. A documented relationship is not automatic proof of attribution in a new incident.

practicals.title: Trace a group
practicals.description: Trace one group to techniques and software.
steps: Record three technique relationships and one software relationship.
Write what the relationships do and do not prove.
practicals.solution: Use the current group page and relationship evidence.

quiz.question: What does a group-technique relationship provide?
quiz.explanation: It encodes documented knowledge, not current compromise.

summary: Use group relationships to form hypotheses, not shortcut attribution.

lessons.title: Mitigations and Defensive Interpretation
lessons.description: Use mitigations as risk-reduction guidance.

notes.text: Mitigations are defensive measures intended to reduce the opportunity or effectiveness of techniques. They are distinct from detections.

practicals.title: Rank mitigations
practicals.description: Select a technique and rank associated mitigations.
steps: Rank by feasibility for a hypothetical organization.
practicals.solution: Use current ATT&CK relationships and justify local ranking; ATT&CK does not provide a universal priority.

quiz.question: What is a mitigation?
quiz.explanation: Mitigations describe defensive measures.

summary: ATT&CK informs controls; local architecture determines priority.

lessons.title: Evidence-First Mapping
lessons.description: Map reports without inventing specificity.

practicals.title: Map a narrative
steps: Create one row per observable behavior.
practicals.solution: Only accept mappings supported by the narrative; preserve rejected hypotheses separately.

quiz.question: What if evidence only supports a broad technique?
quiz.explanation: Specificity should follow evidence.

summary: Good mapping is evidence-led, not box-filling.

tasks.title: Evidence-Backed ATT&CK Mapping
tasks.description: Map a supplied incident narrative with evidence and confidence.
tasks.problemStatement: Produce behavior, ATT&CK ID, rationale, confidence, evidence, and source URL for each defensible mapping.
tasks.hint: Start from the behavior verb and object, not the malware name.
tasks.solutionCode: Use a table or JSON with behavior, attack_id, rationale, confidence, evidence, source_url.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution demonstrates evidence traceability and explicit uncertainty.

modules.title: ATT&CK Navigator and Coverage
modules.description: Operationalize ATT&CK through layers, coverage definitions, and gap analysis.

lessons.title: Navigator Fundamentals
lessons.description: Create and interpret ATT&CK Navigator layers.

notes.text: Navigator provides custom views and annotations of ATT&CK matrices for defensive coverage, threat intelligence, planning, and other uses.
A colored cell is an annotation, not evidence that a technique occurred or is fully detected.

practicals.title: Create an investigation layer
practicals.solution: Use the current Navigator UI and its current layer format.

quiz.question: What is a Navigator layer?
quiz.explanation: Layers are custom views/annotations.

summary: Navigator is a communication artifact; rationale remains essential.

lessons.title: Coverage and Gap Analysis
lessons.description: Define meaningful coverage instead of chasing 100 percent.

items: ATT&CK advises against treating 100% coverage as the universal goal.

practicals.title: Build a coverage scorecard
practicals.description: Score ten techniques across capability states.
practicals.solution: Use a transparent state model such as no telemetry, telemetry only, analytic tested, response tested.

quiz.question: Why not chase 100%?
quiz.explanation: MITRE recommends prioritizing relevant techniques.

summary: Coverage metrics are useful only when the capability being measured is explicit.

lessons.title: Threat Intelligence Layers
lessons.description: Compare adversary profiles visually.

notes.text: Navigator can visualize techniques associated with groups or campaigns. Comparisons should preserve source and time context.

practicals.title: Compare two groups
practicals.solution: Use current group pages; overlap does not prove collaboration.

quiz.question: What can layer comparison show?
quiz.explanation: It supports comparison, not attribution proof.

summary: Layer comparison is useful for communicating threat hypotheses.

lessons.title: Layer JSON and Reproducibility
lessons.description: Treat Navigator layers as auditable data artifacts.

notes.text: Do not place secrets or unnecessary sensitive incident data into shareable layers.
Layer schemas can evolve. Inspect the current Navigator documentation/template before generating production layers programmatically.

practicals.title: Inspect a layer
practicals.solution: Compare the exported structure with the current Navigator documentation.

quiz.question: Why record layer context?
quiz.explanation: Version/domain context makes layers interpretable.

summary: Shareable layers should be reproducible and appropriately sanitized.

modules.title: Detection Engineering with ATT&CK
modules.description: Use the modern defensive model of Detection Strategies, Analytics, and Data Components.

lessons.title: Detection Strategies and Analytics
lessons.description: Understand the defensive model introduced in v18.

notes.text: ATT&CK v18 replaced technique-level detection content with Detection Strategies and Analytics and deprecated Data Sources as the primary defensive model.

items: Analytics provide more specific detection logic.
Data Components express relevant telemetry properties.

practicals.title: Trace a detection strategy
practicals.description: Follow a strategy to analytics and data components.
practicals.solution: Use live relationships and cite exact object pages.

quiz.question: What does a Detection Strategy do?
quiz.explanation: Strategies are high-level detection approaches.

summary: Current defensive work should use the current detection model.

lessons.title: Data Components and Telemetry
lessons.description: Translate defensive requirements into concrete telemetry.

notes.text: Data Components identify specific properties or values relevant to detecting a behavior. They are more granular than the deprecated Data Sources concept.

practicals.title: Build telemetry requirements
steps: List data components for a chosen strategy.
practicals.solution: Start with ATT&CK data components, then document the actual local telemetry implementation.

quiz.question: What do Data Components express?
quiz.explanation: They describe granular evidence needed for detection.

summary: Start with required evidence, then map to actual logs.

lessons.title: From Technique to Analytic
lessons.description: Design testable behavior-based detection.

practicals.title: Design an analytic
practicals.description: Create SIEM-neutral logic for a safe behavior.
practicals.solution: Example: IF process_creation AND suspicious condition AND unexpected parent THEN candidate alert; tune using approved administrative workflows.

quiz.question: Why adapt ATT&CK analytics locally?
quiz.explanation: Local telemetry schemas and workflows differ.

summary: ATT&CK is a behavior model, not a copy-paste SIEM rule repository.

lessons.title: Detection Validation and Tuning
lessons.description: Test positive, negative, boundary, and telemetry-missing cases.

notes.text: Validation asks whether the analytic detects the target behavior, avoids expected benign activity, and provides enough context for investigation.

practicals.title: Create a detection test matrix
practicals.solution: Use synthetic or approved lab events only.

quiz.question: What is a negative test?
options: Benign case that should not alert
quiz.answer: Benign case that should not alert
quiz.explanation: Negative tests measure false positives.

summary: Detection quality requires controlled validation.

tasks.title: ATT&CK Detection Specification
tasks.problemStatement: For a current Enterprise behavior, document Detection Strategy, Analytics, Data Components, hypothesis, logic, exclusions, and tests.
tasks.hint: Start from the current Detection Strategy page.
tasks.solutionCode: Use JSON/Markdown fields attack_id, strategy_id, analytics, data_components, hypothesis, logic, exclusions, tests.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The result demonstrates a complete behavior-to-detection reasoning chain.

modules.title: Threat Hunting and Threat-Informed Defense
modules.description: Build ATT&CK-aligned hypotheses, abstract analytics, hunt priorities, and evidence-backed reporting.

lessons.title: Hunting Hypotheses
lessons.description: Turn ATT&CK behaviors into testable hunt questions.

notes.text: A hunt hypothesis states what suspicious behavior is expected, where it may occur, what evidence should exist, and under what conditions.

practicals.title: Write a hunt hypothesis
practicals.solution: Use: If an adversary uses [behavior] on [platform], we expect [telemetry] under [conditions].

quiz.question: What comes before a hunt query?
quiz.explanation: The hypothesis determines the required evidence.

summary: ATT&CK anchors behavior; local telemetry determines execution.

lessons.title: Abstract Analytics and Behavior Chains
lessons.description: Model multi-event behavior without overfitting to a tool.

notes.text: Abstract analytics describe behavioral conditions independent of a vendor schema. Behavior chains combine multiple observations for context.

practicals.title: Model a behavior chain
practicals.description: Create a three-stage safe simulated chain.
practicals.solution: Use benign/synthetic events; do not conduct unauthorized intrusion.

quiz.question: Why use abstract analytics?
quiz.explanation: Abstract logic can later be implemented in platform-specific forms.

summary: Chains require careful timing and missing-event handling.

lessons.title: Hunt Prioritization
lessons.description: Prioritize hunts using threat relevance, exposure, telemetry, and impact.

notes.text: ATT&CK does not provide a universal organization-specific priority. Local threat intelligence, exposure, telemetry quality, and impact should influence the backlog.

practicals.title: Build a hunt backlog
practicals.solution: Any defined consistent scale is acceptable; explain why the score is actionable.

quiz.question: What should drive local hunt priority?
quiz.explanation: Priority should reflect local risk and feasibility.

summary: Transparent assumptions matter more than arbitrary universal scores.

lessons.title: Hunt Reporting
lessons.description: Report findings with scope, confidence, limitations, and ATT&CK context.

notes.text: A negative result means the behavior was not observed in the searched scope and available telemetry; it does not prove the behavior never occurred.

practicals.title: Write a hunt report
steps: Recommend one detection and one telemetry improvement.
practicals.solution: Use labels such as confirmed, likely, inconclusive, and not observed.

quiz.question: What does a negative hunt result mean?
quiz.explanation: Results are bounded by scope and visibility.

summary: Good reporting makes uncertainty explicit.

modules.title: STIX 2.1, ATT&CK Data, and Automation
modules.description: Use official machine-readable ATT&CK data, relationships, provenance, and acquisition methods.

lessons.title: ATT&CK as STIX 2.1
lessons.description: Understand machine-readable ATT&CK representation.

notes.text: MITRE publishes ATT&CK in STIX 2.1 collections. The machine-readable representation is the granular form from which other views are derived.

items: The ATT&CK Data Model provides schemas and typed tooling.

practicals.title: Inspect a STIX collection
practicals.description: Inventory object types and trace one relationship.
steps: Find a relationship and resolve source/target.
practicals.solution: Use the official repository and preserve the release/version context.

quiz.question: Which STIX type represents a technique?
quiz.explanation: ATT&CK techniques use STIX attack-pattern objects.

summary: Programmatic ATT&CK use benefits from understanding the human-facing catalog and STIX model.

lessons.title: Query ATT&CK with Python
lessons.description: Use safe local parsing to find an ATT&CK technique.

notes.text:
import json
from pathlib import Path
bundle=json.loads(Path("enterprise-attack.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
techniques=[o for o in bundle["objects"] if o.get("type")=="attack-pattern"]
print(len(techniques))

practicals.title: Find a technique by ID
steps: Check external_references for source_name=mitre-attack and external_id.
practicals.solution: Use the external ATT&CK ID instead of object order.

quiz.question: Why use external_references?
quiz.explanation: ATT&CK external IDs are represented in STIX external references.

summary: Avoid hard-coded object positions.

lessons.title: Relationships and Provenance
lessons.description: Resolve Group/Software relationships programmatically.

notes.text: STIX relationships use source_ref and target_ref. An ID index makes traversal efficient and deterministic.

practicals.title: Build an object index
practicals.description: Resolve techniques related to a selected group.
steps: Find relationships from its STIX ID.
practicals.solution: Use a dictionary keyed by STIX id and preserve relationship metadata.

quiz.question: Why index STIX IDs?
quiz.explanation: Relationships point to STIX IDs.

summary: Relationship provenance should be retained in generated outputs.

lessons.title: TAXII and Acquisition Strategy
lessons.description: Distinguish STIX and TAXII and design reproducible acquisition.

notes.text: STIX is a CTI language/serialization format; TAXII is an HTTPS exchange protocol. MITRE documents repository and TAXII access to ATT&CK.

practicals.title: Design an acquisition workflow
practicals.description: Choose sources for current and historical work.
steps: Compare versioned repository data, current repository content, and TAXII.
practicals.solution: Maintain a versioned local cache and record release context for investigations; use live retrieval when appropriate for refresh workflows.

quiz.question: Which statement is correct?
options: STIX is CTI format; TAXII is exchange protocol
quiz.answer: STIX is CTI format; TAXII is exchange protocol
quiz.explanation: They have distinct roles.

summary: Reproducible investigations need versioned content and provenance.

tasks.title: Build an ATT&CK Relationship Query
tasks.description: Create a Python utility that resolves a Group or Software ID to related techniques.
tasks.problemStatement: Given enterprise-attack.json and an ATT&CK external ID, print related attack-pattern IDs, names, and relationship types.
tasks.hint: Build STIX ID and external ID indexes first.
tasks.solutionCode: Use dictionaries for ID resolution and relationship traversal.
tasks.solutionExplanation: This avoids object-order assumptions and preserves relationship semantics.

modules.title: Adversary Emulation, Purple Teaming, and Legacy Migration
modules.description: Use ATT&CK safely for validation and translate older terminology into current defensive concepts.

lessons.title: Adversary Emulation
lessons.description: Understand controlled ATT&CK-based validation.

notes.text: Use only isolated, authorized environments. Course exercises should prefer benign simulation or synthetic telemetry over real destructive tooling.
MITRE emulation plans use public threat reporting and ATT&CK to help defenders test networks and products against modeled adversary behavior.

practicals.title: Design a safe emulation plan
practicals.solution: Prefer synthetic events or benign administrative actions that create comparable telemetry.

quiz.question: What is the defensive purpose of emulation?
quiz.explanation: Emulation validates defensive capabilities.

summary: The value is measurement, not destructive execution.

lessons.title: Purple Teaming
lessons.description: Coordinate emulation and defense around shared behavior.

notes.text: Purple teaming uses shared objectives between simulation and defense teams. ATT&CK provides common behavior terminology for planning and reporting.

practicals.title: Create a purple-team test card
practicals.solution: Results should be detected, partially detected, not detected, or inconclusive with evidence.

quiz.question: Why is ATT&CK useful to purple teams?
quiz.explanation: ATT&CK creates a common vocabulary.

summary: Each test should end with evidence and an improvement action.

lessons.title: Threat-Informed Defensive Backlog
lessons.description: Convert ATT&CK findings into measurable improvements.

notes.text: Threat-informed defense uses adversary knowledge to improve controls. ATT&CK organizes behavior; local risk determines priority.

practicals.title: Create improvement tickets
practicals.solution: Avoid vague actions; tie each ticket to a behavior and testable outcome.

quiz.question: What is a good improvement action?
quiz.explanation: Operationalization requires concrete validation.

summary: ATT&CK matters when it changes capabilities.

lessons.title: Legacy Practices and Migration
lessons.description: Read older ATT&CK reports while using current defensive terminology.
learningObjectives: translate Data Sources to Data Components

notes.text: ATT&CK v18 deprecated Data Sources and introduced Detection Strategies, Analytics, and expanded Data Components. Older reports may still use the previous vocabulary.
Preserve original terminology for historical fidelity, but use current concepts for new workflows.

practicals.title: Migrate a legacy note
steps: Find current Detection Strategy/Analytics where applicable.
practicals.solution: Maintain historical and current interpretation fields.

quiz.question: What changed in v18?
options: Detection Strategies/Analytics introduced; Data Sources deprecated
quiz.answer: Detection Strategies/Analytics introduced; Data Sources deprecated
quiz.explanation: This was a major defensive-model change in v18.

summary: Version-aware translation is necessary for long-lived content.

modules.title: Final Project: ATT&CK Coverage & Threat Mapping Workbench
modules.description: Integrate evidence-based mapping, STIX automation, version awareness, coverage analysis, and Navigator visualization into one defensible workflow.

lessons.title: Capstone Architecture
lessons.description: Design the data flow and evidence model.

items: Observations → ATT&CK dataset → ID resolution → enrichment → report/layer.

practicals.title: Draft capstone schema
practicals.description: Define required fields and acceptance criteria.
practicals.solution: Use the schemas in the project files as the baseline.

quiz.question: What are the two primary inputs?
quiz.explanation: The project combines ATT&CK data with analyst observations.

summary: The architecture keeps evidence and catalog knowledge distinct.

lessons.title: Implement Resolution and Enrichment
lessons.description: Run the included utility and inspect outputs.

notes.text: The implementation uses ATT&CK external IDs for user input and STIX IDs for relationship/object resolution. It is designed for local, reproducible analysis.

practicals.title: Run the workbench
practicals.solution: If the current dataset changes fields, validate the parser against current MITRE documentation before production use.
practicals.output: Report and layer files are produced.

quiz.question: Why use external ATT&CK IDs?
options: They are stable user-facing identifiers for catalog objects
quiz.answer: They are stable user-facing identifiers for catalog objects
quiz.explanation: External references connect human-facing ATT&CK IDs to STIX objects.

summary: Automation should fail clearly on unresolved IDs.

lessons.title: Capstone Audit and Presentation
lessons.description: Validate technical correctness and communicate uncertainty.

practicals.title: Conduct final audit
practicals.solution: Use TEST_PLAN.md and add tests for any release-specific behavior encountered.

quiz.question: What makes the capstone defensible?
quiz.explanation: Defensibility comes from reproducibility and evidence.

summary: The final project demonstrates ATT&CK as an analytical and engineering workflow.

project.name: ATT&CK Coverage & Threat Mapping Workbench
project.description: A realistic defensive capstone combining evidence-backed mapping, STIX 2.1 enrichment, version awareness, coverage reporting, and Navigator visualization using only synthetic or authorized observations.
steps: Download a current or version-pinned Enterprise STIX 2.1 collection from MITRE.
Review the synthetic observations file and replace or extend it only with authorized evidence.
Inspect the report for resolved and unresolved mappings.
Inspect the generated Navigator layer and validate its format against the current Navigator documentation.
Run the test plan and record failures.
Record the exact dataset version/retrieval context in the final submission.

code.README.md:
# ATT&CK Coverage & Threat Mapping Workbench
A defensive capstone using a local MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise STIX 2.1 collection and synthetic/authorized observations. It resolves ATT&CK IDs, enriches observations, produces a reviewable report, and creates a Navigator layer artifact. It does not execute malware, exploit systems, or collect credentials.
code.TEST_PLAN.md:
# Test Plan
1. Use a current or deliberately version-pinned Enterprise ATT&CK STIX 2.1 collection from MITRE.
2. Run the utility with the included synthetic observations.
3. Add an invalid ATT&CK ID and confirm it becomes unresolved.
4. Add a duplicate observation and confirm the report counts observations while the layer keeps one technique entry.
5. Parse both generated JSON files.
6. Inspect the generated layer against the current ATT&CK Navigator documentation before production use.
7. Confirm the project performs no unauthorized network interaction or offensive execution.

project.explanation: The workbench reads a machine-readable ATT&CK dataset and analyst observations. It indexes STIX IDs and ATT&CK external IDs, resolves observations to attack-pattern objects, extracts tactic context, writes a reviewable report, and produces a compact Navigator layer artifact. The workflow demonstrates evidence → mapping → enrichment → visualization → audit. It intentionally avoids malware execution, exploitation, credentials, or unauthorized interaction. The generated layer must be checked against the current Navigator schema before production use because tooling formats can evolve.
